summary:
SARrealists is an interactive web experience that makes NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data understandable to non-experts. A Mapbox globe takes visitors through three regions: California (wildfire scars and Central Valley subsidence), the Himalayas (glacier change and GLOF risk) and the Nile Delta (soil moisture and coastal subsidence). Regional analysis pages show NISAR-derived layers. Captain DIO, a bilingual (English/Arabic) pixel-art game, teaches players which SAR measurements answer which questions. LUMEN, an AI assistant, explains the data for four audiences (scientist, decision maker, student, enthusiast), with answers grounded in curated NASA/NISAR sources. 

NISAR sees through cloud, smoke and darkness and detects centimetre-scale ground motion, but its products are large and technical. By turning them into a story, a game and a conversation, SARrealists shows why radar matters, including for food security and subsidence in Egypt’s Nile Delta.
details:
What it does and how it works

SARrealists turns NISAR radar data into an experience people can scroll through, play and question. It has four parts that reinforce each other.

1. A data pipeline. A Python pipeline searches ASF DAAC with asf_search and streams only the area of interest from each NISAR granule (about 7 GB each) instead of downloading it whole. It computes calibrated layers from the GCOV, GUNW and SME2 products and exports Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs, plots, GeoJSON and a catalog. The website reads these exports directly.

2. A scrollytelling globe. A full-screen Mapbox globe walks visitors through California (wildfire scars and Central Valley subsidence), the Himalayas (glacier change and GLOF risk) and the Nile Delta (soil moisture and coastal subsidence). Each region has a human character and a scientist guide. A Mission Control Dashboard then lets visitors explore freely, jumping between regions, toggling NISAR layers and switching HH/HV polarization. Three regional analysis pages go deeper into the physics and the data.

3. The Captain DIO game. Captain DIO is an astronaut who lands on an Earth-like planet and uses a SAR satellite to protect his crew. The player goes through four missions. In each one they read a briefing and choose two SAR “lenses” (for example, which polarization or product to analyse) to answer the mission’s question. The engine scores the quality of that choice. A good choice keeps the crew safe, while a poor one leaves crew members injured and out of action, so every pick has a visible cost. Crew state carries across missions and ends in a final mission report, and the player’s best report is saved. A lens codex explains each radar measurement in plain language, so the game doubles as a reference. At the end the player learns the planet was Earth all along and is invited to explore the real data. Before that reveal the story deliberately avoids real place names and coordinates, so the twist works. The game has 22 original pixel-art mission images, plus pixel-art charts, sprites and crew portraits. It is fully bilingual (English and Arabic, with right-to-left layout), supports keyboard play and reduced motion, and has optional looping theme music.

4. LUMEN, an AI assistant. It is available on every page and has four personas: Scientist, Decision Maker, Student and Enthusiast. The question, persona, language and optional map-click context go to a server-side route, which applies a small rate limit. LUMEN retrieves matching chunks from a curated NASA/NISAR source set, builds a grounded prompt, and gets an answer from a Gemini or OpenAI-compatible model. The answer comes back with sources and confidence notes. With no model key configured, a local grounded fallback answers from the bundled references and labels itself as such.

Benefits and intended impact

NISAR will produce an enormous amount of freely available data, but most of its potential value is lost if only specialists can read it. SARrealists lowers that barrier in three ways.

  • Understanding: students and the public learn what radar can see that cameras cannot, such as burn scars under smoke, millimetre-scale ground motion, and soil moisture from space. They learn it by doing, not by reading a definition.
  • Relevance: the Nile Delta story ties NISAR to food security and coastal subsidence in our own region. The Arabic interface means the content reaches people who rarely get Earth-observation material in their language.
  • Decision-making: a decision maker can ask LUMEN what a layer means for their question, in plain terms and with sources, without becoming a radar expert first.
  • Support for the mission: missions like NISAR depend on public understanding and support. People who have “used” the data are more likely to see why it was worth building.

We also see the project as reusable. The pipeline and site structure can take new regions, and the game’s content is data-driven, so educators could adapt missions to other sites.

Tools

  • Web: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Mapbox GL, Recharts, Framer Motion, Zod
  • Data: Python, asf_search, COG/Zarr export, Google Colab for heavy processing
  • AI: a Gemini or OpenAI-compatible model for LUMEN, behind a server-side route
  • Quality: Vitest, pytest, a content-validation script
  • Hosting: Vercel, with GitHub and jsDelivr serving the data export

Creativity

Instead of building another viewer, we built a narrative. Real-feeling people guide each region, the game makes the choice of SAR lens a decision with consequences, and the final reveal makes players realise that the story was about their own planet. LUMEN adapts its explanation to who is asking.

Factors we considered

  • Data size and bandwidth: streaming only the area of interest, with heavy processing moved to Colab.
  • Accessibility: Arabic with RTL support, keyboard-accessible controls and reduced-motion support.
  • Trust: grounded, cited AI answers, and automated tests for the game, content and LUMEN. A validation script also stops the game’s pre-reveal content from leaking place names.
  • Honesty about limits: the regional pages use static exports, some game visuals are illustrative placeholders, and nothing here is an operational hazard or alert service.
